rationale: This 2004 paper examines private sector participation (privatization, greenfield projects, concessions, leases, operation and management contracts and outsourcing) in the water and wastewater utilities sector, noting customer service improvements alongside social and economic concerns tied to water as a basic human necessity, as well as global trade and investment patterns. Because utility ownership and concession/contractual structures are squarely within scope of Criterion 2, and the unstructured abstract does not make clear whether the full text contains empirical analysis/case-study data (c3) measuring household water/sanitation access, coverage or affordability outcomes (c4) versus a non-empirical trade/market overview, the protocol rule against prematurely excluding ambiguous utility-governance abstracts requires an 'unsure' verdict for full-text retrieval.
plain_vs_narrow_note: No divergence in overall Phase 5 disposition (both 'unsure'). Privatization, concessions, leases and operation and management contracts clearly constitute institutional/contractual governance forms under plain Criterion 2 ('yes') and fall within the narrow Criterion 2 utility-ownership/regulatory-structure category if examined as mechanisms governing service access ('unclear' from the abstract whether linked to access versus international trade/investment). Under both readings, full-text review is required to determine whether the paper reports primary empirical evidence (c3) and household/community service-access outcomes (c4).

evidence_quotes.quote: Countries introduce private sector participation into the water and wastewater utilities sector for a number of reasons.

Private participation in the global water and wastewater industry can take a number of forms- including privatization, greenfield projects, concessions, leases, operation and management contracts, and outsourcing- and most countries employ a mix of methods.
However, because water is a basic human necessity, the introduction of private participation in this industry sector may raise social, economic, and national security concerns.
